A parameter the control unit reports that this app has no decoder for. The raw value is shown as the car sent it, without a formula or a unit behind it. Treat it as a curiosity rather than a diagnosis.

The difference between pressure in the intake manifold and the air pressure outside, so it shows how much the turbo or supercharger is actually adding. On a naturally aspirated engine it stays at or below zero, because the throttle can only ever restrict. It is computed here from manifold and barometric pressure, not read as its own sensor. Most factory turbocharged engines peak somewhere around 0.5–1.5 bar of boost, and a car that no longer reaches its usual peak has a leak or a boost control problem to find.

How much fuel the engine is burning right now, in litres per hour. Most cars do not report it directly, so it is usually estimated from air flow and the mixture — good enough to compare driving styles, not to settle an argument about the tank. At idle a small petrol engine sits near 0.5–1.5 L/h.

Instantaneous consumption: the current fuel rate divided by the current speed. It swings wildly by design — it goes to infinity when the car stops and near zero when coasting in gear — so it is read as a trend over a few seconds, not as a single number. For an average over a drive, use the trip summary instead.

Voltage measured by the adapter itself at the OBD socket, not by the car. With the engine off it is the resting battery, typically 12.4–12.7 V; with the engine running it is the charging system, typically 13.8–14.6 V. A resting reading under about 12.2 V suggests a discharged or tired battery, and a running reading that stays near 12 V suggests the alternator is not charging.

How hard the engine is working, as a percentage of the torque it could make at these revs. The ECU calculates it from air flow, so it is not a throttle position: cruising gently sits around 20–40 per cent, and full throttle approaches 100 per cent. It is the figure most fuel and ignition maps are indexed on.

Temperature of the coolant leaving the engine, measured at the cylinder head. After warm-up a modern engine holds 80–100 °C and the thermostat keeps it there; brief rises when climbing or sitting in traffic are normal. A reading that stays low suggests a stuck-open thermostat, and one climbing well past 105 °C is worth stopping for.

The instant correction the ECU is applying to the fuel it injects, in percent, based on what the oxygen sensor sees right now. It flickers constantly by design — that flicker is closed-loop control working. Sustained values beyond about ±10 per cent mean the base fuelling is off and the ECU is compensating.

The long-term correction the ECU has learned and stored for the fuel map, in percent. It moves slowly and survives a restart, so it is the honest summary of how far off the base fuelling has drifted. Sustained values beyond about ±10 per cent usually point to a vacuum leak, a fuel delivery problem or a drifting mass air flow sensor.

The same instant fuel correction as bank 1, but for the second bank of cylinders — only engines with two cylinder heads, such as a V6 or a flat four, report it. A large and persistent difference between the two banks is more informative than either number alone, because it points at something on one side only.

The learned, stored fuel correction for the second bank of cylinders. Read it next to bank 1: both drifting the same way suggests something common to the whole engine, such as air metering or fuel pressure, while one bank alone suggests an injector, a leak or a sensor on that side.

Pressure in the low-pressure fuel line, referenced to the intake manifold. It matters most on port-injected petrol engines, where it typically sits around 300–400 kPa (3–4 bar) and should hold steady; a weak pump or a clogged filter shows up here as pressure that sags under load. Direct-injection engines usually report the far higher rail pressure separately.

Absolute pressure in the intake manifold, measured against vacuum rather than against the air outside. At idle it sits well below atmospheric — roughly 25–45 kPa — because the closed throttle is holding a vacuum, and at full throttle it approaches the outside air pressure, or exceeds it on a boosted engine. This is not boost: for that, the barometric reading has to be subtracted.

Crankshaft speed in revolutions per minute, reported by the ECU from the crank sensor. A warm petrol engine idles around 600–900 rpm, and a cold one deliberately higher for the first minute or two. An idle that wanders or hunts is usually an air leak, a dirty throttle body or an idle control problem.

Road speed as the car itself measures it, from the wheel or gearbox sensors — not from GPS. It is usually a little optimistic by design, since manufacturers must never under-read, so it can sit a few percent above a satellite reading. Fitting non-standard tyre sizes shifts it further.

How many crankshaft degrees before top dead centre the spark fires. The ECU advances it for efficiency and pulls it back when it detects knock or when the engine is under heavy load, so a figure that drops sharply under acceleration is the knock control doing its job. Light cruise typically shows a lot of advance, 25–40°.

Temperature of the air entering the engine, measured in the intake tract. It tracks the outside air on the move and climbs when the car stands still and heat soaks into the intake. Colder air is denser, so this figure feeds directly into how much fuel the ECU decides to inject. On the move it should settle within about 10–15 °C of the outside air; a reading that stays far above that suggests heat soak that never clears or a drifting sensor.

Mass of air entering the engine, in grams per second, straight from the air flow sensor. It is the primary input for how much fuel to inject, so a sensor drifting low makes the whole engine run lean. A healthy small petrol engine reads roughly 2–5 g/s at idle and tens of grams at full throttle.

How far the throttle plate is open, read at the plate itself rather than at the pedal. On a drive-by-wire car the ECU moves the plate, so this does not have to follow the pedal — it idles at a few percent and can open on its own during warm-up or with the air conditioning on.

Seconds since the engine last started, counted by the ECU. It resets on every start, which makes it useful for telling whether a reading has had time to stabilise — coolant temperature, fuel trims and readiness monitors all mean more after a few minutes than after ten seconds.

Distance driven since the check engine light came on. It stays at zero on a healthy car and keeps counting while a fault is active, so a large number means a fault has been ignored for a long time. Clearing the codes resets it.

Fuel rail pressure measured relative to the intake manifold, so it reflects the pressure difference the injectors actually work against. Port injection systems typically hold a few hundred kPa here and should keep it steady as load changes.

Fuel pressure at the injectors measured against a vacuum reference, which is how direct-injection systems report their high-pressure side. Values in the thousands of kPa are normal there; the ECU raises pressure with load and a rail that cannot follow the demand usually shows up as a fuel-pressure fault code.

How far the ECU has asked the exhaust gas recirculation valve to open, as a percentage. It is a command, not a measurement of the valve — the valve can be commanded open and be stuck shut with soot. EGR is normally closed at idle and under full throttle, and opens during light cruise.

The gap between the opening the ECU asked of the exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) valve and the position it actually sees, as a percentage of the demand. Near zero means the valve is following orders; a persistently large error is the classic signature of a valve clogged with carbon or a failing position sensor.

How far the ECU has opened the purge valve that draws petrol vapour from the charcoal canister into the engine. It is a command rather than a flow measurement. Purging normally happens under light cruise with a warm engine, and a valve stuck open can upset the mixture at idle.

How full the tank is, as a percentage, from the same float sender that drives the dashboard gauge. It is coarse and it sloshes: expect it to move in steps and to read differently on a slope. Use it for trends, not for calculating exactly how many litres are left.

How many complete warm-up cycles the engine has done since the fault codes were last cleared. A warm-up cycle means the coolant rose far enough above its starting temperature, so this is the counter that decides when old codes and readiness monitors finally age out. Low numbers after a clear are normal.

Distance driven since the fault codes were last cleared. It is the honest answer to \"how long has this car been driven since somebody reset it\" — a car with a freshly cleared memory and only a few kilometres on this counter has not yet had a chance to prove anything.

Pressure inside the sealed fuel vapour system, measured against the air outside and reported in pascals. The ECU uses it to test the system for leaks, which is what the evaporative monitor does. Small swings with temperature are normal; a system that will not hold any pressure difference points at a loose fuel cap or a cracked hose.

Air pressure around the car, in kilopascals. It sits near 101 kPa at sea level and falls with altitude — roughly 90 kPa at a thousand metres. The ECU needs it to know how much oxygen the air actually holds, and this app subtracts it from manifold pressure to get boost.

Temperature inside the catalytic converter on bank 1, at the first sensor position. A working converter runs hot — several hundred degrees once lit off — because oxidising what the engine did not burn releases heat. Unusually high readings can mean fuel is being burned in the converter rather than in the cylinder.

The same catalyst temperature for bank 2, on engines with two cylinder banks and two converters. Comparing the two banks is the useful part: a large steady difference points at one side running differently from the other.

Catalyst temperature at the second sensor position on bank 1, further downstream than the first. Read together with the upstream figure it shows how much heat the converter is generating along its length.

Catalyst temperature at the second sensor position on bank 2, which only engines with two cylinder banks report. Like the other catalyst probes it runs at several hundred degrees once the converter has lit off. It is most useful read next to the matching bank 1 figure, where a large steady difference points at one side running differently.

Supply voltage as the engine control unit measures it at its own connector. It is close to the adapter\'s socket reading but not identical, because it has the car\'s wiring between it and the battery. A running engine should show the charging system here, typically 13.5–14.6 V.

How much air the cylinders are actually taking in, as a percentage of a full, unboosted fill — which is why it can exceed 100 per cent on a boosted engine while calculated load cannot. It is the better number for comparing how hard the engine is breathing across different revs, because it does not scale itself to what is possible at the moment.

The air-fuel mixture the ECU has asked for, expressed as lambda where 1.000 is the chemically ideal ratio. This is a command, not a measurement: it says what the ECU wants, while the wide-range sensor says what it got. In closed loop it sits at 1.000 and it goes rich under full throttle.

Throttle opening expressed against the closed position the ECU has learned, so it starts from zero when your foot is off the pedal. It is easier to read than the absolute figure, which never quite reaches zero because the sensor has an offset.

Outside air temperature as the car measures it, usually from a sensor behind the bumper. It lags reality when the car has been standing in the sun and settles once moving. The ECU uses it for climate control and for density corrections.

The reading from the second throttle position sensor. Drive-by-wire throttles carry two sensors that must agree, and the ECU compares them constantly — a disagreement between them is what triggers limp mode rather than either value on its own.
The reading from a third throttle position sensor, on the systems that fit one. Like the other channels it exists for cross-checking rather than for driving anything directly.

How far the accelerator pedal is pressed, from the first of its sensors. On a drive-by-wire car this is your input and the throttle plate position is the ECU\'s response to it, so the two can differ legitimately.
The second accelerator pedal sensor. The pair exists for safety: the ECU only accepts a pedal request that both sensors agree on, and a mismatch is what puts the car into reduced power.
A third accelerator pedal sensor, where one is fitted. It serves the same cross-checking role as the other two channels.

The throttle opening the ECU has commanded the actuator to take, as opposed to the position the plate reports. Comparing the two is a direct check on whether the throttle body is doing what it is told.
How many minutes the engine has run with the check engine light on. Together with the distance counter it separates a fault that appeared on the last trip from one that has been lit for months.

Engine running time since the fault codes were last cleared. Readiness monitors need a certain amount of running to complete, so a small figure here explains why a car is not yet ready for an emissions test.

What the ECU believes it is burning — petrol, diesel, LPG and so on — as a coded value. It is a declaration from the control unit rather than a measurement, and this app uses it to pick the right constants when estimating fuel rate from air flow.

How much ethanol the fuel contains, as a percentage, on cars with a flex-fuel sensor. The ECU needs it because ethanol needs more fuel for the same air, so the whole fuelling strategy shifts with this number.

Vapour system pressure reported on an absolute scale rather than against the outside air. It carries the same information as the relative reading but never goes negative, which makes it easier to log across changing weather.
The wide-range version of the vapour pressure reading, covering a larger span than the fine-resolution one. Cars that run large-leak and small-leak tests report both, each suited to a different test.

Absolute fuel rail pressure, measured against vacuum rather than against the manifold. Direct injection systems report thousands of kPa here and vary it with load; a rail that cannot reach its target is a common cause of rough running under acceleration.
Accelerator pedal position expressed against the released position the ECU has learned, so it reads zero with your foot off. It is the pedal equivalent of the relative throttle figure.

How much useful life the hybrid battery pack has left, as a percentage, as the ECU estimates it. It is not the state of charge and it does not move as you drive; it is a slow health estimate that declines over years.

Engine oil temperature as the control unit reports it. Oil warms more slowly than coolant and settles higher, typically 90–110 °C in normal driving, and it is the better guide to whether the engine is truly warm. Sustained readings well past 120 °C shorten oil life.

The crank angle at which fuel injection is timed, in degrees. It matters on direct-injection and diesel engines, where moving injection earlier or later changes combustion noise, emissions and how much of the charge burns.

Fuel consumption in litres per hour, reported by the ECU itself rather than estimated. Where a car supports it, this is the more trustworthy of the two figures, because the ECU knows exactly how long it held the injectors open.

The torque the driver has asked for, as a percentage of the engine\'s reference torque. Multiply it by the reference figure to get newton metres. Compared with the delivered value it shows whether anything is limiting the engine.

The torque the engine is actually delivering, as a percentage of its reference torque. A persistent gap below the demanded figure means something is limiting output — knock control, a boost fault, or a deliberate protection strategy.

The engine\'s rated maximum torque in newton metres, which the percentage torque readings are scaled against. It is a fixed property of the engine, not a live measurement, so it does not change as you drive.

Mass of exhaust leaving the engine, in kilograms per hour. It follows air flow closely, since almost everything that goes in comes out, and aftertreatment strategies use it to work out how much they have to clean.

The gear ratio the gearbox reports — engine speed divided by output shaft speed — rather than the gear number on the dash. It is only meaningful while the car is moving: at a standstill the output shaft is not turning, so the ratio is undefined and the value parks at a placeholder.

Total distance the car has travelled, as the control unit holds it. Not every car exposes it, and where it does the figure should track the instrument cluster closely. It is the reading worth logging at the start and end of a trip.

Output voltage of a narrow-band oxygen sensor in the exhaust. It is a switch rather than a scale: around 0.1 V means lean, around 0.9 V means rich, and a healthy sensor before the catalyst swings between them several times a second. A sensor after the catalyst should instead sit fairly still around the middle, which is how a working converter shows itself.

The signal voltage from a wide-range oxygen sensor. It is not the 0.1–0.9 V switch a narrow-band sensor makes: a wideband probe reports its measurement as lambda, and this channel is the raw electrical signal behind it. Read the lambda channel for the mixture itself.

The fuel correction being applied on account of this particular oxygen sensor, in percent. It is the same idea as the bank fuel trim but attributed to one probe, which is what makes it useful on an engine with several sensors: it says which one the ECU is reacting to.

The mixture as a wide-range oxygen sensor actually measured it, where 1.000 is the chemically ideal air-fuel ratio. Below 1.000 is rich and above it is lean. Unlike the commanded value this is a measurement, so the difference between the two is the fuelling error the ECU has not corrected yet.

The pump current a wide-range oxygen sensor draws to hold its measuring cell at the reference mixture. It is how the sensor physically works rather than a reading to interpret directly — near zero means the exhaust is already at lambda 1, and the sign tells you which way it is off.

The instant fuel correction derived from the oxygen sensor behind the catalyst, in percent. The downstream sensor trims slowly and gently, because its job is to fine-tune what the upstream sensor is doing, not to control fuelling on its own. Large values here often accompany a tired converter.

The learned, stored correction derived from the oxygen sensor behind the catalyst. It drifts slowly over many drives and survives a restart, so a large stored value is a longer-standing story than the instant one — commonly an ageing converter or a lazy downstream sensor.

Mass of air entering the engine measured by one of the air flow sensors, in grams per second. Engines with two intake tracts report a sensor each; the pair should read closely together at the same load, and a persistent difference points at one sensor or one intake path.

Coolant temperature from one of the engine\'s coolant sensors. Cars with more than one measure at different points in the circuit, so the readings need not match exactly — the difference between them is what tells you about flow and thermostat behaviour.

Intake air temperature at one specific point in the intake tract, identified by bank and sensor number. Where a car reports several, the difference between the one nearest the inlet and the one nearest the engine is intake heat soak, which climbs when the car sits still and falls again on the move.

Temperature of the recirculated exhaust gas at one sensor position. It rises when the EGR valve is actually flowing, which makes it the practical check that recirculation is happening at all: a valve commanded open that produces no temperature rise is a valve that is not flowing.

Back pressure in the exhaust on one bank. It rises with engine load and with anything that restricts flow downstream, so a reading that climbs over time on a diesel usually means the particulate filter is loading up.

How fast the turbocharger shaft is spinning, in revolutions per minute. Turbos run in the tens of thousands of rpm and each has a limit the ECU protects; the figure is most interesting alongside boost pressure, since a turbo spinning hard without making pressure suggests a leak between it and the engine.

Temperature of the compressed intake air after the intercooler, at one sensor position. Compressing air heats it and the intercooler\'s whole job is to take that heat back out, so this reading is the direct measure of how well it is working — it climbs during sustained full throttle and falls again with airflow through the cooler.

Exhaust gas temperature at one sensor position, identified by bank and sensor number. These sensors protect the turbo and the aftertreatment from heat, and on a diesel they climb sharply during a particulate filter regeneration — which is the expected behaviour, not a fault.
open loop or closed loop, as a code

Which mode the fuelling is being controlled in, as the code the standard defines: 1 is open loop because the engine is still cold, 2 is closed loop with the oxygen sensors in charge, 4 is open loop under load or on the overrun, 8 is open loop because something has failed, and 16 is closed loop with a faulty sensor. A warm engine should sit at 2 almost all the time, so one that keeps dropping back to 1 or 8 is worth looking into.
how many probes the exhaust really has

How many oxygen sensors the exhaust actually has, counted from the map the ECU publishes of which of the eight possible positions are filled. It is worth reading because the supported-parameter list routinely offers all eight and then says nothing for the six that do not exist. This is the car\'s own answer, and the app uses it to stop asking after probes that were never fitted.
the gear the car is asking for

The gear the ECU would like you to be in: the shift indicator on the dashboard, and not the gear the gearbox is actually in. Cars that show an arrow telling you to change up are showing this number. For the gear currently engaged, read the gear ratio instead.
the diesel preheat light, on or off

Whether the glow plug warning lamp is lit, as a single on-or-off value. On a diesel it comes on with the ignition while the plugs preheat and goes out once the engine is ready to be started. A lamp still lit after the engine has started is not asking you to wait — it is reporting a fault in the preheat circuit.
whether the box is out of gear

Whether the gearbox reports itself as out of gear, as a single on-or-off value. The ECU uses it to decide how to hold the idle and to tell a stop from a coast. Only cars that publish the signal report it at all, so on the rest this reading is absent rather than false.
the auxiliary drive, on vehicles that have one

Whether a power take-off is engaged — the auxiliary drive a van or a truck uses to run a tipper, a pump or a compressor off the engine. Almost no car has one fitted, so on a car this reading is simply absent.
what the engine spends turning itself

The torque the engine uses up overcoming its own friction and driving its accessories, as a percentage of its reference torque. It is highest on a cold engine full of thick oil and falls as everything warms through, which makes it a quiet indication of how freely the engine is turning over.

Fuel the engine is burning measured as mass rather than volume, in grams per second. It is the figure the litres-per-hour reading is worked out from, and it is the fair one to compare between engines: a litre of diesel weighs more than a litre of petrol, so mass is the common ground.
everything on board that burns fuel

Fuel the whole vehicle is burning, including anything that is not the engine — a fuel-fired cabin heater, for instance. On a car with nothing else drawing from the tank it reads the same as the engine figure, and a lasting difference between the two is that other consumer.
what the oil pump is actually making

Engine oil pressure as the control unit measures it, in kilopascals. Most cars only have a warning lamp for this, and by the time the lamp is on the answer is already bad news; this is the number behind it. At a warm idle most engines hold roughly 100–200 kPa (1–2 bar), rising to several bar at higher revs and falling as hot oil thins. The reading worth remembering and comparing year on year is the one at a warm idle.
oil heat, from the maker\'s own sensor

Oil temperature read from the manufacturer\'s own parameter rather than the standard one, which many cars do not answer. Oil warms more slowly than coolant and settles higher, usually between 90 and 110 °C, and it is the better guide to whether the engine is genuinely warm enough to be worked hard.
how hot the gearbox oil is

Temperature of the fluid inside an automatic gearbox, read from the transmission control unit. In ordinary driving it settles around 70–100 °C, and it is the number that decides when the torque converter is allowed to lock up. Sustained readings past about 120 °C are what shorten a gearbox\'s life — towing up a long hill is the classic way to get there.
the pressure the wheel sensor reports

Pressure inside one tyre, as its own sensor reports it to the body module. The dashboard warning only appears once a tyre is well down, so having the four numbers is what turns a slow puncture into something you notice in a week rather than a month. Pressure rises by a tenth of a bar or so as the tyres warm up, which is why they are set cold.
how warm the wheel sensor is running

Temperature measured inside one wheel by the same sensor that reports its pressure. It rises with speed and with an underinflated tyre flexing, so one wheel running consistently warmer than the others is worth a look — and it explains why that corner\'s pressure reads higher after a motorway run.
how far up the sensor the oil stands

The height of the oil in the sump, measured by the level sensor the dipstick was replaced with, in millimetres above the sensor\'s zero. It is not a litre count and it only settles once the engine has been off for a few minutes on level ground — but read the same way each time, it turns "am I using oil?" into a number that answers itself over a few thousand kilometres.
what the turbo is actually delivering

Pressure in the inlet manifold as the engine\'s own sensor reports it, measured against vacuum rather than against the air outside. About 1 bar at idle is the weather, not the turbo; what the turbo adds is everything above that, so 2.2 bar absolute on full throttle is roughly 1.2 bar of boost. A turbocharged engine that will not reach the boost it used to has a leak, a wastegate or a set of vanes to answer for.

Temperature of the air after the turbocharger has compressed it and the intercooler has done what it can, measured just before it enters the engine. Compression heats air, so this climbs steeply under load and falls again with airflow; a charge that stays hot on the move is an intercooler that is blocked, leaking or full of oil.

Temperature of the cylinder head casting itself, which Ford control units read directly. It reacts faster than the coolant gauge and keeps reading after the coolant has boiled or leaked away, which is exactly why it is fitted: an engine losing coolant shows it here first, while the temperature gauge is still sitting reassuringly in the middle.
how hard the turbo is being held back

How much the control unit is commanding the wastegate actuator, as a percentage of its full travel. Low figures mean the turbo is being allowed to blow off exhaust and make less boost; a car that needs an ever-higher duty cycle to reach the same boost is losing the ability to hold it — a leaking pipe, a tired actuator or a sticking valve.
the twist the engine says it is making

Torque at the flywheel as the control unit\'s own model works it out, in newton metres. It is a calculation rather than a measurement — no production car has a torque sensor — but it is the number the engine, the gearbox and the stability system all negotiate with, and watching it against the throttle shows where a torque limit is being applied.
total distance, from the car itself
which gear the gearbox is in

The car\'s own accumulated distance, read out of the module that keeps it rather than off the dashboard. Worth having for two reasons: it dates every other reading in this app against the car\'s life, and a figure that disagrees with the instrument cluster is the loudest thing a used car can say about itself.

The gear the transmission itself reports, read from the gearbox control unit rather than worked out from speed and revs. This is the trustworthy version of the gear on the dashboard: the estimate has to assume the torque converter is locked, and on an automatic in town it often is not. Park, reverse and neutral are not forward gears, so the reading is simply absent in them.
what the charging system is producing

Electrical power the alternator is delivering, in watts. It rises when the battery is low or the heated screen is on and falls to almost nothing on a full battery at cruise, which is the engine being spared the work. An alternator that never comes down is charging a battery that will not hold, and one that never goes up on a cold morning is not charging at all.
refrigerant pressure on the high side

Pressure of the refrigerant, which is what the climate control watches before it decides whether to run the compressor at all. With the system off it settles at a pressure that follows the outside temperature; a system that reads far below that when everything is at rest is a system that has lost gas, which is why the air conditioning stopped working long before anybody added dye.
how much exhaust is being fed back

How far the exhaust gas recirculation valve is being held open, as a percentage. Recirculated exhaust cools combustion and cuts the oxides of nitrogen a diesel makes; it also carries soot back into the inlet, which is why the valve and the manifold behind it eventually clog. A valve commanded open that never moves is the classic cause of a limp-home diesel.
the geometry that makes low-down boost

Position of the variable vanes inside the turbocharger, as a percentage of their travel. Closing them speeds the exhaust up and makes boost at low engine speed; opening them lets a big turbo breathe at the top end. Vanes that soot up and stick are the reason a diesel goes flat or surges, and they show here as a position that will not follow the command.
how far this injector is off the others

How much fuel this cylinder is being given above or below the average of the others, in milligrams per stroke, so that all four run equally. The engine works this out from how each cylinder accelerates the crankshaft. Three near zero and one drifting steadily away is a worn or leaking injector named out loud, months before it becomes a rough idle and a fault code.
how full the starter battery is

State of charge of the twelve-volt battery, as the car\'s own battery sensor keeps it. This is not a voltage reading: the sensor tracks every amp that has gone in and out since the battery was last fitted, which is how the car decides whether stop-start is allowed. A battery that sits below about seventy per cent after a long drive is one that is no longer taking the charge it is offered.
how much of a new battery is left

The battery sensor\'s own verdict on how much capacity the battery still has against the capacity it had when new, as a percentage. It falls slowly over years and then quickly in one cold winter. It is the number to write down each autumn: a battery that has lost a quarter of itself will start the car all summer and refuse on the first frosty morning.
how warm the starter battery is

Temperature of the twelve-volt battery, measured at the sensor clamped to its terminal. Cold batteries deliver less and accept charge more slowly, which is why the car raises its charging voltage in winter, and a battery in a hot engine bay ages faster than the same one under a seat. It is context for every other battery reading rather than a fault of its own.
measured at the battery, not the socket

Voltage at the battery itself, as the car\'s own sensor measures it. The adapter\'s reading is taken at the diagnostic socket at the end of a length of wiring, so it reads a little lower under load; this one is the honest figure. Resting, a healthy battery sits near 12.6 V; with the engine running the charging system holds it between about 13.5 and 14.8 V.
charging in, or being drawn out

Current flowing in or out of the twelve-volt battery, positive one way and negative the other. It is the reading that finds a parasitic drain: with everything off and the car properly asleep, a healthy vehicle draws well under a tenth of an amp, and anything above that is a module that has not gone to bed and will flatten the battery over a fortnight of standing.
the ageing a voltmeter cannot see

Internal resistance of the twelve-volt battery in milliohms, which is the measurement that catches a battery on its way out. Resistance rises as the plates age and the acid stratifies, and it is what decides whether the battery can deliver the hundreds of amps a cold start asks for. A healthy starter battery measures only a few milliohms, and a value several times that is a battery near the end — one can read a perfect 12.7 V at rest and still fail here.
soot the pressure sensor can see

How much soot is in the diesel particulate filter, worked out from the pressure difference across it, in grams. It climbs through short cold journeys and drops sharply when the car burns the filter clean at speed. Watching it is what tells a driver why the car keeps starting a regeneration, and comparing it against the calculated figure is how a blocked filter is told apart from a lying pressure sensor.
soot the engine believes it has made

The control unit\'s own model of how much soot the filter holds, in grams, worked out from the fuel burnt and the conditions it was burnt in rather than from a sensor. The car regenerates on whichever of the two figures reaches its limit first. A steady gap between this and the measured value is the interesting part: the model and the sensor disagreeing means one of them is wrong.
the part that never burns off

Incombustible ash accumulated in the particulate filter, in grams. Soot burns away in a regeneration; ash — the residue of engine oil additives — does not, and it fills the filter permanently over the car\'s life. It is the number that says whether a filter is temporarily full or genuinely at the end, and the honest answer to "will another forced regeneration fix it?"
how far since the last burn-off

Distance driven since the particulate filter last burnt itself clean. A healthy diesel used on longer journeys goes several hundred kilometres between regenerations; a car doing short cold trips can be starting one every fifty, which is how unburnt fuel ends up in the sump and why the oil level slowly rises. It is the single most useful number a diesel driver can watch.

How many times the car began burning the filter clean and was stopped before it finished — almost always by the engine being switched off at the end of a short journey. Each interruption leaves the filter fuller than it started and brings the next attempt forward. A count that keeps climbing is a car being asked to do the wrong sort of driving.
exhaust heat going into the filter

Temperature of the exhaust gas entering the particulate filter. Ordinary running puts it a few hundred degrees; a regeneration takes it past 600 °C, which is what it takes to burn soot away, and that is why the car asks to be driven at a steady speed and why nobody should park over dry grass immediately afterwards. It is also the clearest way to see that a regeneration is happening.

Temperature of the exhaust gas leaving the particulate filter. During a regeneration it runs above the inlet, because the soot burning inside is itself a fire; the difference between the two is the burn happening. Outside a regeneration the two sit close together and the outlet is the cooler of the two.
how hard the exhaust has to push

Difference in pressure between the two ends of the particulate filter, which is the measurement every soot estimate is built on. It is near zero at idle whatever the filter is like — it takes flow to show a restriction — so it means something only under load, where a rising figure at the same engine speed is a filter that is filling up.
the real state of charge, not the gauge

State of charge of the high-voltage battery as its own management computer holds it. On a hybrid this is the figure behind the dashboard\'s little bar chart, and it moves within a band the car keeps deliberately narrow — a hybrid that runs its pack from full to empty would wear it out in a year. On an electric car it is the number the range estimate is made from.
capacity left against when it was new

How much of its original capacity the high-voltage battery still has, as a percentage. It is the single most valuable number about a used electric or hybrid car and the one no advertisement carries: two identical cars with the same mileage can be ten points apart, and ten points is the difference between a winter commute that works and one that does not.

Voltage across the whole high-voltage battery. It rises and falls with the state of charge and sags under hard acceleration, and how far it sags for a given current is a measure of the pack\'s internal resistance — which is the same ageing story the twelve-volt battery tells, on a scale of hundreds of volts.
power out, or regeneration back in

Current flowing out of the high-voltage battery or back into it, positive one way and negative the other. It is the clearest view of a hybrid actually working: hundreds of amps out under acceleration, a steady flow back in on every lift and every brake application, and near zero when the engine is doing the work alone.

Energy currently stored in the high-voltage battery, in kilowatt hours. Against the pack\'s nominal size it is the honest measure of what is left in it, and against a trip\'s distance it is what consumption per hundred kilometres is worked out from — the electric car\'s equivalent of litres in the tank.
the electronics between battery and motor

Temperature of the coolant running through the power electronics that turn the battery\'s direct current into the alternating current the motor uses. It has a cooling circuit of its own, separate from the engine\'s and usually cooler; a hybrid that quietly stops giving full electric assist on a hot day is often one whose inverter is protecting itself.
Only the run counters were reported
Every self-test is inside its limits
the car sent no pass limits for this test

Oxygen storage is how much oxygen the converter can still hold, and it falls slowly over a converter\'s life. The ECU sets P0420 when it drops below the limit shown here, so a figure creeping towards that limit over several readings is the warning that arrives months before the light does.
How often each monitor has run
Each pair is how many times the self-test finished against how many times the car was driven in the conditions it needs. A monitor that has never finished has not passed — it has not been tried.
